screens.title: Chain of Responsibility
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will explore the Chain of Responsibility pattern and why it matters when a request might be handled by different components. The core idea is simple: let many objects have a chance to handle a request without the sender needing to know which one will do it. You can think of a customer support ticket that escalates from Level 1 to Level 2, and then to a specialist. That movement is the chain in action. We will learn the roles in the pattern — an abstract handler, concrete handlers, the successor reference, and the request itself — and see a concrete C# logging example where console, file, and email handlers each decide whether to act. You will also practice building a small expense-approval chain where different managers approve amounts up to their limit. Along the way we will point out common pitfalls, such as silent unhandled requests and chains that grow too long. By the end you will understand how to compose handlers dynamically, avoid tight coupling, and choose sensible defaults so requests aren’t lost. Consider how a request flows: who inspects it, who acts on it, and when it should be forwarded. That understanding is the chapter’s practical payoff.

screens.title: Why decouple senders and receivers?
screens.narratorSegment: The Chain of Responsibility answers a clear design problem: how can a sender issue a request without needing to know which component will handle it? The solution is to give the request to an entry handler and let it travel through a chain until some handler processes it. Imagine a customer support flow: the client submits a ticket to Level 1. If Level 1 can solve it, the ticket is closed. If not, Level 1 forwards it to Level 2, and so on. This removes the need for the client to choose the correct team and prevents early handlers from hard-coding knowledge about every later handler. As a concrete example from the chapter, a logging system can send a single message to the chain. A ConsoleLogger might always write Info messages, a FileLogger might write Warning and above, and an EmailLogger might trigger for Critical. A common misconception is that only one handler should process a request. In many logging examples, multiple handlers act on the same message — Console and File may both write it. The pattern supports either single handling or multiple processing depending on how HandleRequest is implemented. The key takeaway is: decoupling increases flexibility and makes adding or reordering handlers a runtime choice rather than a code change. How would you decide whether a request should be processed by one handler only or by several?

keyIdea.title: Decoupling defined
keyIdea.text: Senders rely on an entry point only; the chain determines which handler(s) process the request.

content.html:
Core Concept
Why decouple senders and receivers?
Avoid making the client responsible for routing requests to specific handlers. Let handlers forward requests until one can act.
Explanation
  • The client sends to the chain entry point only; it doesn't know handler details.
  • Handlers contain focused logic and a reference to their successor to forward requests.
  • Adding, removing, or reordering handlers is a runtime operation, not a code rewrite.
Analogy
Support ticket escalations: Team A tries first, and if unresolved, passes to Team B, then to a specialist.
Key Takeaway

Decoupling via a chain reduces tight coupling and centralizes forwarding logic, making systems easier to extend.

Customer Support Flow (visual)
Request submitted
Level 1: First responder
Attempts resolution. If not handled, forwards to next successor.
Level 2: Escalation
Has deeper expertise. May handle or forward to specialist.
Specialist
Final attempt. If unhandled, a default path or alert is needed to avoid silent failure.

screens.title: Pattern structure: Handler, Successor, Request
screens.narratorSegment: To implement the Chain of Responsibility you need three core elements: an abstract handler interface or base class, concrete handler implementations, and a successor reference that links handlers into a chain. The abstract handler declares a method to process requests and a method to set the next handler in the chain. Each concrete handler knows only its own responsibility — for example, a FileLogger handles Warning-level messages — and a reference to its successor so it can forward requests it cannot fully satisfy. The request is simply the data passed into HandleRequest, for instance a log level and message, or an Expense object with amount and description. A common misconception is that the abstract handler must include complex logic; it should be minimal: a constructor for configuration, a SetNext method that returns the successor for fluent chaining, and a HandleRequest method that either handles or forwards. This minimal design keeps handlers focused and makes chain wiring straightforward. As a mental check, ask: does each handler know only what it must handle and how to forward? If yes, you have the correct separation of concerns.

content.html:
Definition
Pattern structure
Minimal parts you must implement to build a working chain.
Abstract Handler
Declares SetNext and HandleRequest. Stores configuration such as the level it handles.
Concrete Handler
Implements WriteMessage or handling logic for the request it is responsible for.
Successor
A reference to the next handler; SetNext returns the successor to allow fluent wiring.
Request details
A request carries the data the handlers need. Examples: a log level and message, or an Expense with amount and description.
Concrete example
LogHandler stores a LogLevel threshold and passes the message to successor regardless, or conditionally depending on desired behavior.
Misconception
Handlers are not responsible for knowing the whole chain. They only need to know their successor to forward requests.
Key Takeaway

Keep handler APIs small: configuration, SetNext, and HandleRequest are sufficient for most uses.

screens.title: Building the chain with SetNext
screens.narratorSegment: A practical design detail is how handlers are linked. The chapter illustrates SetNext returning the successor so you can write fluent code like handler1. SetNext(handler2). SetNext(handler3). This pattern is convenient when building fixed chains in Main or during configuration. When you call SetNext, you simply assign the successor reference and return it so the next SetNext call targets that successor. The fluent style reads naturally and keeps wiring code concise. Importantly, chains can be reconfigured at runtime. For example you might build a chain for normal operation and replace a handler with a monitoring handler for debugging without changing handler implementations. A concrete example: in a logging chain, you might insert a DatabaseLogger between FileLogger and EmailLogger to persist warnings during a maintenance window. A common mistake is assuming SetNext also changes behavior — it only sets forwarding. Behavior comes from each handler's HandleRequest. Finally, think about ownership: ensure the chain is built in a deterministic place in your app, such as startup code, and document the intended order so future changes remain predictable. Building the chain with SetNext means setnext returns the successor to enable concise, readable chain construction and supports runtime reconfiguration.. In practical terms, fluent chain construction and runtime flexibility. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Fluent wiring
keyIdea.text: SetNext returns the successor to enable concise, readable chain construction and supports runtime reconfiguration.

content.html:
Process Flow
Building the chain with SetNext
Use SetNext to link handlers; return the successor to allow fluent chaining.
Steps to build a chain
  1. Instantiate handlers with their configuration (levels, names).
  2. Call SetNext to assign the successor and return it for chaining.
  3. Send requests to the first handler only; it will forward as needed.
Runtime reconfiguration
You can reorder or replace handlers at runtime to change processing order without modifying handler code.
Key Takeaway

Keep chain wiring in a single startup location and use SetNext for clear, maintainable configuration.

Example wiring
// Pseudocode-style C# wiring (conceptual)
var consoleLogger = new ConsoleLogger(LogLevel.Info);
var fileLogger = new FileLogger(LogLevel.Warning);
var emailLogger = new EmailLogger(LogLevel.Critical);

consoleLogger.SetNext(fileLogger).SetNext(emailLogger);

// Send messages to consoleLogger.HandleRequest(level, message);
This example shows fluent chaining. The client only calls HandleRequest on the entry handler.

screens.title: C# LogHandler: core methods
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the LogHandler abstraction and its HandleRequest behavior shown in the chapter. The abstract class holds a LogLevel threshold and a successor reference. SetNext assigns the successor and returns it, enabling fluent chaining. HandleRequest compares the incoming level with the handler's configured level. If the message meets or exceeds the threshold, the handler writes the message through its WriteMessage implementation. The chapter shows that after writing, the handler still forwards the request to its successor if one exists. This illustrates a design choice: handlers may process and still forward so multiple handlers can act on one request. An alternative is to forward only when the handler does not process the request, enforcing single handling. Both are valid; choose based on requirements. A concrete example from the text: ConsoleLogger handles Info and above, FileLogger handles Warning and above, and EmailLogger handles Critical. When you send a Critical message, all three may act if HandleRequest forwards regardless. A common pitfall is failing to escape unhandled requests: if the chain ends and no handler processed it, decide whether to log, throw, or use a default handler. That decision affects system safety and observability.

keyIdea.title: HandleRequest behavior
keyIdea.text: Handlers can both process and forward requests; decide whether your design allows multiple handlers acting on one request or enforces single handling.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Abstract LogHandler
Core fields: successor reference and configured level. Core methods: SetNext and HandleRequest.
public abstract class LogHandler
{
    protected LogHandler _successor; // next handler
    protected LogLevel _level;       // threshold

    public LogHandler(LogLevel level)
    {
        _level = level;
    }

    public LogHandler SetNext(LogHandler successor)
    {
        _successor = successor;
        return successor; // fluent wiring
    }

    public void HandleRequest(LogLevel level, string message)
    {
        if (level >= _level)
        {
            WriteMessage(message);
        }

        if (_successor != null)
        {
            _successor.HandleRequest(level, message);
        }
    }

    protected abstract void WriteMessage(string message);
}
Explanation and choices
This implementation processes if level meets threshold, then forwards regardless. That lets multiple handlers act. If you need only one handler to process, change forwarding to be conditional when not processed.
Concrete example
Sending Critical will trigger ConsoleLogger, FileLogger, and EmailLogger if each writes and still forwards.
Key Takeaway

Decide whether handlers should forward after processing or only when they skip processing; align the choice with system requirements.

screens.title: Concrete handlers: Console, File, Email
screens.narratorSegment: Concrete handlers implement the abstract handler's contract and define the real side effects for a request. In the chapter's logging example, ConsoleLogger writes to standard output, FileLogger would append to a file, and EmailLogger triggers alerts. Each handler is configured with a minimum LogLevel it will process. For instance ConsoleLogger can accept Info and above, FileLogger Warning and above, and EmailLogger Critical and above. A key observation from the example is that these concrete handlers remain simple: they only implement WriteMessage and rely on the base class for forwarding. A common contrast is whether handlers should be stateful or stateless. Logging handlers are often stateless: they write and return. Approval handlers like TeamLead or DepartmentManager may be stateful if they record approvals. Another important detail is that the same request can be processed by multiple handlers — the logger example intentionally lets all eligible handlers act. But some domains require single handling, such as when a ticket must be claimed by exactly one agent; in that case the forwarding logic must stop after a handler processes the request. The practical rule is to design handlers to match your domain semantics and keep side effects explicit and testable.

keyIdea.text: Keep concrete handlers focused: implement the handling action and rely on the base class for forwarding behavior; choose stateful or stateless based on domain needs.

content.html:
Comparison
Concrete handlers
ConsoleLogger, FileLogger, and EmailLogger illustrate different side effects for the same request.
ConsoleLogger
Quick output for Info and above; useful for development and immediate feedback.
FileLogger
Persists Warning and above to storage for auditing; typically writes to a file or persistent sink.
EmailLogger
Triggers alerts for Critical events; may be rate-limited or guarded to avoid alert storms.
Design considerations
  • Decide if requests may be handled by multiple handlers or only a single one.
  • Make side effects explicit and easily testable in each concrete handler.
  • Consider fallback or default handlers to avoid silent failures.
Example scenario
A Critical log could be written to console, appended to a file, and also trigger an email alert; keep each action isolated in its handler.

screens.title: Expense approval workflow (starter code)
screens.narratorSegment: The hands-on activity asks you to implement a simple expense approval workflow using the Chain of Responsibility. The starter code defines an Expense type and an abstract Approver class with a SetNext method and an abstract ProcessRequest method. Your task is to create three concrete approvers: TeamLead approves expenses up to one hundred dollars, DepartmentManager up to one thousand dollars, and CEO for anything above. Each approver checks the expense amount: if it's within their limit, they call expense. Approve with their name; otherwise, if a successor exists, they call _successor. ProcessRequest(expense); if no successor exists, they print that the expense cannot be approved. This structure keeps approval logic isolated to each role and allows easy changes to approval limits or order. A common mistake is to forget to call SetNext and therefore have the chain end prematurely. Another is to mix approval logic with chain wiring; keep responsibilities separate by building the chain in Main. When you run the examples provided in the starter code, compare the output with the expected approvals in the chapter to confirm correct behavior.

screens.title: Common mistakes and safe guards
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter highlights several pitfalls to watch for when using the Chain of Responsibility. First, unhandled requests: if a request reaches the end of the chain with no handler processing it, it may silently fail. Defenses include adding a default handler at the chain's end, logging an explicit error, or throwing an exception to surface the condition. Second, chains that are too long can introduce performance overhead due to repeated traversals. If many handlers execute per request, measure and limit work per handler or collapse responsibilities where appropriate. Third, unintended repeated processing occurs when handlers both process and forward a request but the domain expects only one handler to act. Decide up front whether multiple handlers should handle the same request and enforce that in HandleRequest logic. A fourth issue is improper wiring: forgetting to call SetNext means parts of the chain are unreachable. Build the chain in a single startup place and add tests that verify the sequence. Finally, be mindful of side effects in handlers — for example, sending duplicate alerts — and design handlers to be idempotent or guarded.

content.html:
Common Pitfalls
Unhandled requests and performance
These issues can turn a clean design into a maintenance burden if not addressed.
Unhandled requests
Add a default handler or explicit reporting so requests that reach the chain's end are visible.
Long chains
Too many handlers can slow processing. Measure and collapse stages when overhead is high.
Repeated processing
Decide whether multiple handlers should act on one request and implement forwarding accordingly.
Improper wiring
Ensure SetNext is called correctly and test the chain sequence during startup.

  • Add a default handler that logs or escalates unhandled requests.
  • Use metrics to detect slow chains and optimize accordingly.
  • Make side effects idempotent to prevent duplication across handlers.

Protect against silent failures with a default path, keep chains focused, and test wiring to ensure predictable behavior.

screens.title: Testing and safe defaults
screens.narratorSegment: Robust Chain of Responsibility implementations include tests and safe defaults. First, add unit tests that verify chain wiring: ensure SetNext was called and that requests reach the expected handlers. Test both single-handling and multi-handling scenarios depending on your design. Second, provide a default handler at the chain's end that logs or raises an explicit error when requests are unhandled; this prevents silent failures. Third, instrument handlers to emit metrics so you can detect expensive chains or unexpected traversals. Fourth, make handler side effects idempotent or guarded to prevent duplicate effects when multiple handlers may act on the same request. For example, avoid sending repeated alerts for the same Critical event by centralizing alert deduplication. Finally, keep chain construction centralized so reconfiguration is easier and tests can instantiate the same wiring. screens.title: Dynamic configuration and entry points
screens.narratorSegment: An advanced usage the chapter mentions is dynamic configuration: handlers can be added, removed, or reordered at runtime. You may also expose multiple chain entry points depending on request type. For example, urgent tickets can bypass Level 1 by sending the request directly to Level 2's handler. This keeps handlers unchanged and lets the client choose the correct entry point. Runtime reordering can be achieved by holding a configurable list of handlers and rebuilding the chain when configuration changes. This is useful for feature flags or seasonal behavior when you want to insert a monitoring handler temporarily. A trade-off is increased complexity in ensuring thread-safe modifications and maintaining predictable ordering. Tests that simulate reconfiguration and verify that outstanding requests behave correctly are vital. As an example, the chapter suggests inserting a DatabaseLogger into a logging chain during maintenance; after the window, remove it. When you design for dynamic configuration, plan for safe updates, consistent ordering, and clear documentation so team members understand where the chain is built and how to modify it. In this lesson we will explore the Chain of Responsibility pattern and why it matters when a request might be handled by different components. The core idea is simple: let many objects have a chance to handle a request without the sender needing to know which one will do it. You can think of a customer support ticket that escalates from Level 1 to Level 2, and then to a specialist. That movement is the chain in action. We will learn the roles in the pattern — an abstract handler, concrete handlers, the successor reference, and the request itself — and see a concrete C# logging example where console, file, and email handlers each decide whether to act. You will also practice building a small expense-approval chain where different managers approve amounts up to their limit. Along the way we will point out common pitfalls, such as silent unhandled requests and chains that grow too long. By the end you will understand how to compose handlers dynamically, avoid tight coupling, and choose sensible defaults so requests aren’t lost. Consider how a request flows: who inspects it, who acts on it, and when it should be forwarded. That understanding is the chapter’s practical payoff.

These objectives focus your work on understanding the pattern and applying it in C#. First, you will understand the purpose of the Chain of Responsibility: how it decouples the sender from the receiver so a request can be escalated without the client knowing the final processor. Second, you will identify scenarios where a request might need multiple potential processors, such as logging levels or multi-stage validation. Third, you will implement the pattern in C# using an abstract handler and concrete classes, practicing SetNext and HandleRequest. Fourth, you will explain how requests are passed along the chain until handled or exhausted, and how to avoid common pitfalls like unhandled requests. Each objective pairs a coding skill with a practical reason why it matters, so you can build flexible, maintainable pipelines and workflows.

These additional objectives tie the concept to concrete practice. You will construct example chains like a multi-level logging pipeline and an expense approval workflow so you can see handlers working together. You will reason about dynamic configuration: how to reorder or swap handlers at runtime to change behavior without modifying handler code. You will also practice spotting common mistakes such as chains that grow unnecessarily long or missing a fallback handler, and learn mitigations such as default handlers or explicit reporting for unhandled requests. Finally, you'll explain the pattern's trade-offs and identify when a chain is a better fit than alternatives. These outcomes ensure you can both build and critique Chain of Responsibility implementations in real systems. Apply and practice means build a logging chain and an approval workflow, then verify dynamic reconfiguration and safe behavior for unhandled requests.. In practical terms, coding tasks and scenario-based reasoning. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Chain of Responsibility answers a clear design problem: how can a sender issue a request without needing to know which component will handle it? The solution is to give the request to an entry handler and let it travel through a chain until some handler processes it. Imagine a customer support flow: the client submits a ticket to Level 1. If Level 1 can solve it, the ticket is closed. If not, Level 1 forwards it to Level 2, and so on. This removes the need for the client to choose the correct team and prevents early handlers from hard-coding knowledge about every later handler. As a concrete example from the chapter, a logging system can send a single message to the chain. A ConsoleLogger might always write Info messages, a FileLogger might write Warning and above, and an EmailLogger might trigger for Critical. A common misconception is that only one handler should process a request. In many logging examples, multiple handlers act on the same message — Console and File may both write it. The pattern supports either single handling or multiple processing depending on how HandleRequest is implemented. The key takeaway is: decoupling increases flexibility and makes adding or reordering handlers a runtime choice rather than a code change. How would you decide whether a request should be processed by one handler only or by several?

To implement the Chain of Responsibility you need three core elements: an abstract handler interface or base class, concrete handler implementations, and a successor reference that links handlers into a chain. The abstract handler declares a method to process requests and a method to set the next handler in the chain. Each concrete handler knows only its own responsibility — for example, a FileLogger handles Warning-level messages — and a reference to its successor so it can forward requests it cannot fully satisfy. The request is simply the data passed into HandleRequest, for instance a log level and message, or an Expense object with amount and description. A common misconception is that the abstract handler must include complex logic; it should be minimal: a constructor for configuration, a SetNext method that returns the successor for fluent chaining, and a HandleRequest method that either handles or forwards. This minimal design keeps handlers focused and makes chain wiring straightforward. As a mental check, ask: does each handler know only what it must handle and how to forward? If yes, you have the correct separation of concerns.

A practical design detail is how handlers are linked. The chapter illustrates SetNext returning the successor so you can write fluent code like handler1. SetNext(handler2). SetNext(handler3). This pattern is convenient when building fixed chains in Main or during configuration. When you call SetNext, you simply assign the successor reference and return it so the next SetNext call targets that successor. The fluent style reads naturally and keeps wiring code concise. Importantly, chains can be reconfigured at runtime. For example you might build a chain for normal operation and replace a handler with a monitoring handler for debugging without changing handler implementations. A concrete example: in a logging chain, you might insert a DatabaseLogger between FileLogger and EmailLogger to persist warnings during a maintenance window. A common mistake is assuming SetNext also changes behavior — it only sets forwarding. Behavior comes from each handler's HandleRequest. Finally, think about ownership: ensure the chain is built in a deterministic place in your app, such as startup code, and document the intended order so future changes remain predictable. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through the LogHandler abstraction and its HandleRequest behavior shown in the chapter. The abstract class holds a LogLevel threshold and a successor reference. SetNext assigns the successor and returns it, enabling fluent chaining. HandleRequest compares the incoming level with the handler's configured level. If the message meets or exceeds the threshold, the handler writes the message through its WriteMessage implementation. The chapter shows that after writing, the handler still forwards the request to its successor if one exists. That decision affects system safety and observability.

Concrete handlers implement the abstract handler's contract and define the real side effects for a request. In the chapter's logging example, ConsoleLogger writes to standard output, FileLogger would append to a file, and EmailLogger triggers alerts. Each handler is configured with a minimum LogLevel it will process. For instance ConsoleLogger can accept Info and above, FileLogger Warning and above, and EmailLogger Critical and above.
